'''Charles Peter DeLisi''' (born December 9, 1941) is an American [[biomedical scientist]] and the Metcalf [[Professor]] of Science and Engineering at [[Boston University]]. He is noted for major contributions to the initiation of the [[Human Genome Project]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=President Clinton Awards the Presidential Citizens Medals|url=https://clintonwhitehouse5.archives.gov/WH/new/html/Mon_Jan_8_141714_2001.html|access-date=2020-09-05|website=clintonwhitehouse5.archives.gov|archive-date=2017-08-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828012148/https://clintonwhitehouse5.archives.gov/WH/new/html/Mon_Jan_8_141714_2001.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> for transformative academic leadership,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bu.edu/eng/profile/charles-delisi-ph-d/|title=Charles DeLisi, Ph.D. &#124; College of Engineering|website=www.bu.edu|access-date=2020-07-25|archive-date=2020-09-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919113302/https://www.bu.edu/eng/profile/charles-delisi-ph-d/|url-status=live}}</ref> and for research contributions to mathematical and computational immunology,<ref name="DeLisiBerzofsky1985">{{cite journal|last1=DeLisi|first1=C.|last2=Berzofsky|first2=J. A.|title=T-cell antigenic sites tend to be amphipathic structures.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=82|issue=20|year=1985|pages=7048–7052|issn=0027-8424|doi=10.1073/pnas.82.20.7048|pmid=2413457|pmc=391307|bibcode=1985PNAS...82.7048D|doi-access=free}}</ref> cell biophysics,<ref>DeLisi, C., and Blumenthal, R. (Ed.): Physical Chemical Aspects of Cell Surface Events in Cellular Regulation. New York, Elsevier, North Holland, 1979</ref> genomics<ref name="KanethisaKlein1984">{{cite journal|last1=Kanethisa|first1=Minoru|last2=Klein|first2=Petr|last3=Greif|first3=Peter|last4=DeLisi|first4=Charles|title=Computer analysis and structure prediction of nucleic acid and proteins |journal=Nucleic Acids Research|volume=12|issue=1Part1|year=1984|pages=417–428|issn=0305-1048|doi=10.1093/nar/12.1Part1.417|pmc=321015|pmid=6546426}}</ref><ref name="ReferenceA"/> and protein<ref name="KleinKanehisa1985">{{cite journal|last1=Klein|first1=Petr|last2=Kanehisa|first2=Minoru|last3=DeLisi|first3=Charles|title=The detection and classification of membrane-spanning proteins|journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Biomembranes|volume=815|issue=3|year=1985|pages=468–476|issn=0005-2736|doi=10.1016/0005-2736(85)90375-X|pmid=3838905}}</ref> and nucleic acid<ref>DeLisi, C. and Crothers, D.M., Prediction of RNA Secondary Structure, Proc Nat Acad. Sci,  68, 2682-2685, 1972</ref><ref>Nakata, K., Kanehisa, M., DeLisi, C. Prediction of Splice Junctions in mRNA, Nucleic Acid Research, 13(14), 5327-5340, 1985</ref> structure and function. Recent activities include mathematical finance<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.denovoanalytics.com/about-us|title=Team|website=De Novo Analytics|access-date=2021-04-16|archive-date=2021-04-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210416221348/https://www.denovoanalytics.com/about-us|url-status=live}}</ref> and climate change.<ref>DeLisi, C., Patrinos, A., MacCracken, M., et al The Role of Synthetic Biology in Atmospheric Greenhouse Gas Reduction, AAAS BioDesign Research, Volume 2020 |Article ID 1016207 | https://doi.org/10.34133/2020/1016207 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240429191202/https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/2020/1016207 |date=2024-04-29 }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
DeLisi was born in the Bronx, graduated from [[City College of New York]] (CCNY) with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in history (1963), and received his [[Ph.D.]] in physics (1965 -1969) from [[New York University]] (NYU).<ref name=mathgene>{{MathGenealogy}}</ref>

==Career and research==
In 1969, he joined [[Donald Crothers]]’ laboratory as a [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) [[postdoctoral]] [[research fellow]] in the department of chemistry at [[Yale University]]. In 1972, he was appointed a theoretical division staff scientist at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], where he collaborated with [[George Irving Bell|George Bell]], a theoretical physicist who a few years earlier had begun pioneering research in mathematical immunology. DeLisi was subsequently appointed senior scientist (1975–1982) at the [[National Cancer Institute]], NIH, and founding head of the Section on Theoretical Immunology (1982–1985), where he and his collaborators established one of the earliest protein and DNA sequence databases fully integrated with machine learning programs for functional inference<ref name="KanethisaKlein1984" /> and developed a number of analytical methods that proved useful in cell biology.<ref name="DeLisiBerzofsky1985" /><ref name="CornetteMargalit1995">{{cite journal|last1=Cornette|first1=J. L.|last2=Margalit|first2=H.|last3=Berzofsky|first3=J. A.|last4=DeLisi|first4=C.|title=Periodic variation in side-chain polarities of T-cell antigenic peptides correlates with their structure and activity.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=92|issue=18|year=1995|pages=8368–8372|issn=0027-8424|doi=10.1073/pnas.92.18.8368|pmid= 7667297 |pmc=41158|bibcode=1995PNAS...92.8368C|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="KleinKanehisa1985"/>

In 1986, as director of the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Health and Environmental Research Programs, DeLisi and his advisors proposed the [[Human Genome Project]] to the White House [[Office of Management and Budget]] and the [[United States Congress|Congress]]. The proposal created much controversy but received strong endorsement from [[Alvin Trivelpiece]], who was chief of DOE's Office of Science, and [[William Flynn Martin]], the [[United States Deputy Secretary of Energy|Deputy Secretary of Energy]]. It was included in [[Presidency of Ronald Reagan|President Ronald Reagan]]'s fiscal year 1987 budget submission to the Congress and was approved subsequently by both the House of Representatives and the Senate, the latter with the essential endorsement of Senator [[Pete Domenici]] (R, NM). 
During the spring of 1987, shortly before leaving the DOE, DeLisi established an ethical studies component of the Project.<ref>Robert Cooke-Deegan, Gene Wars, p 262, W. H. Norton, New York, 1994.</ref> The goal was to reserve 3-5% of the funding for scholars of the humanities and social sciences to develop a system of ethics that would inform decisions about the development and deployment of the radically new technologies destined to emerge from the completion of the Project.

In addition to the medical and scientific advances engendered by the Human Genome Project, it and its progeny have had a profound effect on research of cell biology. Computer scientists, in particular, transformed the topic and created a record of discovery destined to provide much material for studying the sociology of late 20th and early 21st century science. Computational and mathematical methods are now considered as important to progress in cell biology, a change that is forcing even the most conservative universities to develop new methods of biological education.<ref>C DeLisi, A Time to Abandon Hedgehogs, Genome Technology, 2001.</ref> The Human Genome Project enabled a rapid transformation of DOE's health, environmental and energy programs, increasing considerably the importance of the Office of Health and Environmental Research.

Commemorating the significance of the Human Genome Project, the DOE installed a bronze plaque outside room F-202 at its [[Germantown, Maryland]] facility. The plaque is imprinted:<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=CharlesDeLisi|title=English: A tribute to the person who launched the Human Genome Project|date=2002-03-01|url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Plaque_commemorating_the_Human_Genome_Project,_outside_Charles_DeLisi%27s_former_office_at_DOE.png|access-date=2020-08-30|archive-date=2024-04-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240429190957/https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Plaque_commemorating_the_Human_Genome_Project,_outside_Charles_DeLisi%27s_former_office_at_DOE.png|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{blockquote|From this room the Human Genome Project evolved from a mere concept to a revolutionary research program through the vision and determination of Dr. Charles DeLisi, Associate Director of Energy Research for Health and Environmental Research, 1985 to 1987.|author=|title=|source=}}

In 1987, DeLisi returned to New York as a professor and department chairperson at the [[Mount Sinai School of Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=DeLisi|first=Charles|date=1988|title=The Human Genome Project: The ambitious proposal to map and decipher the complete sequence of human DNA|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27855388|journal=American Scientist|volume=76|issue=5|pages=488–493|jstor=27855388|issn=0003-0996|access-date=2020-09-03|archive-date=2020-11-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201117014133/https://www.jstor.org/stable/27855388|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Boston University years===

In 1990 DeLisi joined [[Boston University]] (BU) as dean of the College of Engineering.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thetatauarchives.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/2016-psi-delta-bu.pdf|title=BU Theta tau brochure|last=|first=|date=|website=www.thetatauarchives.org|access-date=2020-07-25|archive-date=2020-07-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724021248/http://www.thetatauarchives.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/2016-psi-delta-bu.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Under his watch the College grew into a leading research institution, adding among other things Centers for [[Biotechnology]], [[Photonics]] and [[Manufacturing Engineering]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Charles DeLisi {{!}} College of Engineering|url=https://www.bu.edu/eng/tag/charles-delisi/|access-date=2020-09-05|website=www.bu.edu|archive-date=2021-05-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503191352/http://www.bu.edu/eng/tag/charles-delisi/|url-status=live}}</ref> In addition, the [[Biomedical Engineering]] (BME) department added a new dimension to the field, namely [[Molecular engineering|molecular]] and cellular engineering, and was the home of the seminal research in [[synthetic biology]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gardner |first1=Timothy S. |last2=Cantor |first2=Charles R. |last3=Collins |first3=James J. |s2cid=345059 |title=Construction of a genetic toggle switch in Escherichia coli |journal=Nature |date=January 2000 |volume=403 |issue=6767 |pages=339–342 |doi=10.1038/35002131 |pmid=10659857 |bibcode=2000Natur.403..339G }}</ref>

In 1999 DeLisi initiated the nation's first Ph.D. program in [[bioinformatics]] and served as chairperson for more than a decade.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Boston University's Legacy in Computational, Systems and Synthetic Biology » Computational Genomics Lab {{!}} Boston University|url=http://sites.bu.edu/phenogeno/boston-universitys-legacy-in-computational-systems-and-synthetic-biology/|access-date=2020-09-01|website=sites.bu.edu|archive-date=2020-11-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201109112804/http://sites.bu.edu/phenogeno/boston-universitys-legacy-in-computational-systems-and-synthetic-biology/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2000, after 10 years as dean, DeLisi resumed a full-time faculty position as dean emeritus and Metcalf Professor. The lobby of the building that houses the College of Engineering Dean's Office is named in his honor,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thetatauarchives.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/2016-psi-delta-bu.pdf|title=BU Theta tau brochure|last=|first=|date=|website=www.thetatauarchives.org|access-date=2020-07-25|archive-date=2020-07-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724021248/http://www.thetatauarchives.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/2016-psi-delta-bu.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> as is an annual College of Engineering award lecture.<ref>{{cite web |title=Distinguished Alumna Delivers DeLisi Lecture {{!}} College of Engineering |url=https://www.bu.edu/eng/2022/04/29/distinguished-alumna-delivers-delisi-lecture/ |website=www.bu.edu |access-date=21 January 2021 |archive-date=29 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220429214047/https://www.bu.edu/eng/2022/04/29/distinguished-alumna-delivers-delisi-lecture/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

DeLisi is a [[Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) and of the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]] (AIMBE). In 1999 he was awarded the CCNY [[Townsend Harris]] Medal, in 2011 he was elected an honorary citizen of [[Marineo]], Palermo, Italy,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://win.comune.marineo.pa.it/amministrazione/deliberazioni%20cc%202011/del%20cc%2091.11.pdf |title=Deliberation documents |date=2011 |website=win.comune.marineo.pa.it |access-date=2020-07-25 |archive-date=2020-07-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200723011728/http://win.comune.marineo.pa.it/amministrazione/deliberazioni%20cc%202011/del%20cc%2091.11.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> and in 2019 he was recipient of the [[Informa]] Clinical and research excellence lifetime achievement award.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pharmaintelligence.informa.com/events/awards/care-awards-2019/winners-2019|title=CARE Awards 2019 winners l Pharma Intelligence|website=www.pharmaintelligence.informa.com|access-date=21 January 2021|archive-date=22 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210122104947/https://pharmaintelligence.informa.com/events/awards/care-awards-2019/winners-2019|url-status=live}}</ref>
